planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Joe's Long Cayenne needs a long warm season to fully color and dry its extra-long pods, so an early indoor start pays off.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking plants if pod weight bends the stems. This Calabrian heirloom traveled from Italy to Italian-Canadian growers in Toronto and then to Joe Sestito of Troy, New York, whose name became attached to it when Dr. Carolyn Male introduced the variety to American gardeners through Seed Savers Exchange in 1996. Plants produce heavy clusters of slender, thin-walled cayenne-type pods that can reach up to a foot long, ripening from green to bright red with medium-high heat in the 30,000–50,000 Scoville range. The thin walls make whole pods easy to string into ristras for air-drying, and dried fruit grinds readily into pepper flakes or crushed cayenne.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Joe's Long Cayenne Pepper
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners Database — Cayenne-type Peppers

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant once soil has warmed and nights stay above 55°F. Jwala is a heavy, continuous producer that rewards frequent picking of young green pods.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jwala ('flame' in Hindi) is one of the most widely grown chilies in India, prized as the classic Indian finger hot pepper for everyday cooking. Slender, curved, slightly wrinkled green pods grow 3–4 inches long in dense clusters and carry a fruity, sharp heat (roughly 25,000–50,000 Scoville units) well above a jalapeño. Pods are usually picked and used green — deep-fried whole for the popular mirchi bhaji snack, sliced into curries, or pickled — though left to ripen they turn red and can be dried. Prolific, compact plants perform well in containers as well as garden beds and keep producing through summer heat if picked regularly.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners Database — Jwala Pepper
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Jwala Pepper

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Guntur Chilli needs a long, hot summer to fully redden and dry its pungent pods for storage.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Guntur Chilli is a landrace grown for generations in the Guntur and Prakasam districts of Andhra Pradesh, India, where the Guntur Sannam (S4) type has earned Geographical Indication status and become one of the most heavily traded chili types in the world. Plants bear slender, crimson, thick-skinned pods 2–5 inches long with fierce, wine-red pungency, typically cited in the 35,000–75,000 Scoville range depending on strain and growing conditions. Grown almost exclusively as a drying chile, pods are left to fully redden on the plant, then sun-dried and ground into the vivid, pungent chili powder that underlies much of South Indian cooking. A heavy-yielding, heat-loving plant well suited to long, hot growing seasons.
sources: Geographical Indications Registry of India — Guntur Chilli GI documentation
ICAR–Indian Institute of Spices Research — Guntur Chilli variety notes

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant once soil is warm and nights stay above 55°F. Byadgi needs a long warm season to fully develop its deep red color and thin, wrinkled skin.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Byadgi Chilli takes its name from the town of Byadagi in Karnataka, India, and carries Geographical Indication protection for its distinctive deep red, wrinkled pods. Unlike most chiles grown for pungency, Byadgi is prized above all for color: the slender 2–3 inch pods have a thin, oily skin packed with red pigment but comparatively mild-to-moderate heat, generally cited around 5,000–15,000 Scoville units with a faintly sweet, smoky flavor. Pods are harvested fully red, sun-dried, and used whole or ground to give curries, rasam, and chili powder blends a vivid red color without overwhelming heat. A reliable, productive plant for gardeners who want a true chili flavor and color without intense fire.
sources: Geographical Indications Registry of India — Byadagi Chilli GI documentation
ICAR–Indian Institute of Horticultural Research — Byadgi Chilli variety notes

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant once soil has warmed and frost danger has passed. Chimayó is a high-desert landrace adapted to hot days, cool nights, and low humidity, and it performs best where summer nights cool down rather than staying hot and muggy.

directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Chimayó Chile is a true landrace pepper grown for at least three centuries by Pueblo and Hispanic farming families in the village of Chimayó, in the foothills of New Mexico's Sangre de Cristo Mountains. The thin-walled, 4–6 inch tapered pods ripen from green to deep red and carry a moderate, warming heat (roughly 4,000–6,000 Scoville units) alongside a complex, sweet, smoky flavor that distinguishes it from other New Mexico-type chiles. Pods are traditionally strung into ristras and air-dried, then ground into the red chile powder used for New Mexican posole, carne adovada, and red chile sauce. Because it developed in an isolated, arid high-desert valley, seed-grown plants stay relatively compact and thrive with less humidity and lower water than Gulf Coast or Southeastern pepper varieties.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — Chimayó Chile Variety Notes
Native Seeds/SEARCH — Chimayó Chile Landrace Collection

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. Maraş is grown as a drying pepper, so plan on a full season outdoors for pods to ripen fully red before harvest.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Maraş Pepper is a landrace long grown around Kahramanmaraş in southeastern Turkey, where sun-dried, coarsely crushed pods become the fragrant, oil-glossed red pepper flake known as pul biber. The 3–4 inch, moderately wrinkled pods ripen to a deep brick red and carry a mild-to-moderate heat, generally around 4,000–8,000 Scoville units, with a rich, slightly sweet, faintly smoky flavor distinct from the tangier Aleppo pepper it is often compared to. Traditionally pods are partially sun-dried, seeded, and crushed while still a little moist, which is what gives Maraş flakes their characteristic dark color and oily texture rather than the bone-dry look of standard chili flakes. A single productive plant can supply a household's pepper flakes for a year; harvest fully red pods and dry in a low oven or dehydrator if humid outdoor air prevents full sun-drying.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Kahramanmaraş Pepper
Two Seeds in a Pod — Pul Biberlik Maraş Pepper Seed Notes
